questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q13
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A thin-walled spherical gas balloon of radius \( R \) and wall thickness \( t \) (\( t << R \)) is subjected to an internal (gauge) pressure \( p \). The maximum tensile and shear stresses in the balloon wall are, respectively:
questions.explanation:
Mechanics of Materials | Thin Shells (Spherical Vessels)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension (Bloom's Level 2)
  • Given Data: Spherical balloon of radius \(R\), thickness \(t\), internal pressure \(p\).
  • Aim: Find maximum tensile stress (\(\sigma\)) and maximum shear stress (\(\tau_{\max}\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Tensile Stress in Thin Sphere: Hoop stress = Longitudinal stress = \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \dfrac{pR}{2t}\)
  • In-plane Shear Stress: Since \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2\):
    \(\tau_{\text{in-plane}} = \dfrac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_2}{2} = 0\)
  • Absolute Max Shear Stress (if considering out-of-plane with \(\sigma_3 = 0\)):
    \(\tau_{\text{abs}} = \dfrac{pR/2t - 0}{2} = \dfrac{pR}{4t}\)

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Tensile stress: \(\sigma = \dfrac{pR}{2t}\).
  2. Due to symmetry, any element in the tangent plane experiences zero in-plane shear stress.
  3. Option (B) matches: tensile stress \(\dfrac{pR}{2t}\) and zero in-plane shear stress.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\sigma = \dfrac{pR}{2t}\) and \(\tau = 0\)  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Black dot shown in the figure qualitatively represents the shear centre of the angle section. The option which represents the position of the shear centre is:
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Shear Centre

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension (Bloom's Level 2)
  • Given Data: Visual representation of an L-angle section.
  • Aim: Identify the correct location of the Shear Centre.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Shear Centre: The point through which the resultant of internal shear forces passes. A load applied here causes bending without twisting.
  • Thin-Walled Open Sections: For an angle section, the shear flow in each leg acts along its centerline.
  • Intersection Principle: The shear centre of an angle section lies at the intersection of the centerlines of the two legs.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Observe the L-shape section.
  2. Shear flow in the horizontal leg is horizontal; in the vertical leg, it is vertical.
  3. The moments of these shear flows about the intersection of the two leg centerlines are both zero, meaning the shear resultant passes through this junction.
  4. Option (D) correctly places the shear centre at this intersection point.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Shear centre is at the intersection of the leg centerlines.  |  Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A plane truss consists of two linearly elastic, homogeneous, identical members, namely PQ and QR. Both members have length (L), cross-sectional area (A), and modulus of elasticity (E). The members are inclined at 45° as shown in the figure. The truss has hinge supports at P and R. The translational degrees-of-freedom (u and v) are shown at joint Q.



After application of the boundary conditions, the stiffness matrix of the truss becomes:
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Matrix Methods of Structural Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Plane truss with two identical members PQ and QR.
    • Properties: Length \(= L\), Area \(= A\), Modulus of Elasticity \(= E\).
    • Supports: Hinges at P and R.
    • Geometry: Members are inclined at \(45^\circ\) to the horizontal.
    • Translational DOF at Q: \(u\) (horizontal) and \(v\) (vertical).
  • Aim: Determine the assembled stiffness matrix of the truss at joint Q.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Direct Stiffness Method: Assembly of the global structural stiffness matrix by summing contributions of individual element stiffness matrices at common nodes.
  • Truss Element Stiffness Matrix: The \(2 \times 2\) stiffness sub-matrix at a node is:
    \[K_{\text{local}} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} c^2 & cs \\ cs & s^2 \end{bmatrix}\]
    where \(c = \cos\theta\), \(s = \sin\theta\), and \(\theta\) is the angle measured counter-clockwise from the positive x-axis originating from the node in question.

4. Solution Method:

Since P and R are hinged (zero displacement), we extract sub-matrices at node Q for members QP and QR and add them: \(K_Q = K_{QP} + K_{QR}\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Member QP (from Q to P):
    Direction from Q to P is at \(\theta_{QP} = 225^\circ\).
    \(c = \cos(225^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\quad s = \sin(225^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
    \(c^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad s^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad cs = \dfrac{1}{2}\)
    \[K_{QP} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\]
  2. Member QR (from Q to R):
    Direction from Q to R is at \(\theta_{QR} = 315^\circ\).
    \(c = \cos(315^\circ) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), \(\quad s = \sin(315^\circ) = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)
    \(c^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad s^2 = \dfrac{1}{2},\quad cs = -\dfrac{1}{2}\)
    \[K_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}\]
  3. Assemble the Global Stiffness Matrix at Node Q:
    \[K_{\text{total}} = K_{QP} + K_{QR} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \left( \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & -0.5 \\ -0.5 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \right)\]
    \[K_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{AE}{L} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)  |  Correct option: (C)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The plane frame has a hinge and a roller support, and is loaded as shown in the figure. Both the columns have same height.



What is the absolute value of the maximum bending moment (in kN-m) in the frame?
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Frame Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Plane frame: left support = Hinge (A), right support = horizontal Roller (D).
    • Column height = 3 m; Top beam length = 4 m (2 m + 2 m).
    • Horizontal point load at top-left joint B = 50 kN (\(\rightarrow\)).
    • Vertical point load at beam mid-span E = 90 kN (\(\downarrow\)).
  • Aim: Find the absolute value of the maximum bending moment in the frame (in kN·m).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Static Equilibrium: \(\sum F_x = 0\), \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M = 0\).
  • Support Reactions: Hinge provides \(V\) and \(H\); horizontal roller provides only \(V\).
  • Bending Moment: Computed by evaluating moments from all forces on one side of a section.

4. Solution Method:

  1. Determine support reactions using global equilibrium equations.
  2. Evaluate bending moments at critical locations: Joint B, mid-span load point E, and Joint C.
  3. Identify the maximum absolute bending moment.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify Support Reactions:
    Let A (left hinge) have reactions \(H_A\) and \(V_A\).
    Let D (right roller) have reaction \(V_D\) only (\(H_D = 0\)).
  2. Apply Equilibrium Equations:
    • \(\sum F_x = 0 \Rightarrow H_A + 50 = 0 \Rightarrow H_A = -50\) kN (acts leftward).
    • \(\sum M_A = 0\) (taking clockwise positive):
      \[(50 \times 3) + (90 \times 2) - (V_D \times 4) = 0\]
      \[150 + 180 = 4V_D \Rightarrow V_D = 82.5 \text{ kN (upward)}\]
    • \(\sum F_y = 0 \Rightarrow V_A = 90 - 82.5 = 7.5\) kN (upward).
  3. Evaluate Bending Moments at Critical Points:
    • \(M_A = 0\), \(M_D = 0\) (support ends).
    • At Joint B (top-left):
      \[M_B = H_A \times 3 = 50 \times 3 = 150 \text{ kN·m}\]
    • At Joint C (top-right):
      \[M_C = 0 \text{ kN·m}\]
      (Check from left: \(M_C = (7.5 \times 4) + (50 \times 3) - (90 \times 2) = 30 + 150 - 180 = 0\) ✓)
    • At load point E (mid-span):
      From right: \(M_E = V_D \times 2 = 82.5 \times 2 = 165\) kN·m
      (Check from left: \(M_E = (7.5 \times 2) + (50 \times 3) = 15 + 150 = 165\) kN·m ✓)
  4. Identify Maximum Absolute Bending Moment:
    \(|M_A| = 0\), \(|M_B| = 150\), \(|M_E| = 165\), \(|M_C| = 0\), \(|M_D| = 0\)
    Maximum = 165 kN·m at point E.

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 165 kN·m  |  Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Two identical blocks A and B are connected by a rigid rod. The blocks rest against vertical and horizontal planes, as shown in the figure. The coefficient of static friction at the vertical and horizontal planes is the same. If the sliding impends when \( \theta = 45^\circ \), the value of the coefficient of static friction is _______
(rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
Engineering Mechanics | Friction & Statics

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Two identical blocks (weight \(W\)) connected by a rigid pin-jointed rod at angle \(\theta = 45^\circ\).
    • Identical coefficient of static friction \(\mu\) at both wall and floor.
    • System is at impending slip.
  • Aim: Find the coefficient of static friction \(\mu\).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Impending Motion: Static friction reaches its maximum limit: \(f_s = \mu N\).
  • System Equilibrium: Analyzing blocks + rod as an entire system cancels internal forces and simplifies to global equilibrium (\(\sum F_x = 0\), \(\sum F_y = 0\), \(\sum M_z = 0\)).
  • Kinematics of Slip: Block A slips downwards (friction \(f_A\) points UP); Block B slips rightwards (friction \(f_B\) points LEFT).

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Identify external forces on the system:
    • At Block A: Normal from wall \(N_A\) (\(\rightarrow\)), friction \(f_A = \mu N_A\) (\(\uparrow\)), gravity \(W\) (\(\downarrow\)).
    • At Block B: Normal from floor \(N_B\) (\(\uparrow\)), friction \(f_B = \mu N_B\) (\(\leftarrow\)), gravity \(W\) (\(\downarrow\)).
  2. Force Equilibrium:
    \[\sum F_x = 0 \implies N_A = \mu N_B \quad \cdots (1)\]
    \[\sum F_y = 0 \implies \mu N_A + N_B = 2W \quad \cdots (2)\]
  3. Moment Equilibrium about center of Block B:
    \[\sum M_B = 0 \implies -N_A(L\sin 45^\circ) - f_A(L\cos 45^\circ) + W(L\cos 45^\circ) = 0\]
    Since \(\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ\), divide by \(L\cos 45^\circ\):
    \[W = N_A + f_A = N_A(1 + \mu) \quad \cdots (3)\]
  4. Solve simultaneously:
    From (1): \(N_A = \mu N_B\). Substitute into (3): \(W = \mu N_B(1+\mu)\).
    Substitute into (2): \(N_B(\mu^2 + 1) = 2W\).
    Dividing:
    \[\dfrac{\mu^2 + 1}{\mu(1 + \mu)} = 2 \implies \mu^2 + 1 = 2\mu^2 + 2\mu\]
    \[\mu^2 + 2\mu - 1 = 0\]
  5. Solve the quadratic:
    \[\mu = \dfrac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 4}}{2} = -1 \pm \sqrt{2}\]
    Taking the positive root: \(\mu = \sqrt{2} - 1 \approx 0.414\)

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.41  |  Accepted key range: 0.39 to 0.44

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A homogenous, linearly elastic rod AB is connected to a linearly elastic spring BC in between the fixed supports at A and C, as shown in the figure. The cross-sectional area, modulus of elasticity, and the coefficient of thermal expansion of the rod AB are 500 mm², \( 60 \times 10^3 \) MPa, and \( 12 \times 10^{-6} \) per °C, respectively. The stiffness (k) of spring BC is 2500 N/mm.



The internal force (in kN) that will develop in the spring BC when the temperature of rod AB is increased by 100 °C is _______
(rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Thermal Stresses

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Area of rod: \(A = 500\) mm²
    • Modulus of elasticity: \(E = 60 \times 10^3\) MPa \(= 60{,}000\) N/mm²
    • Thermal coefficient: \(\alpha = 12 \times 10^{-6}\) /°C
    • Spring stiffness: \(k = 2500\) N/mm
    • Length: \(L = 3\) m \(= 3000\) mm
    • Temperature rise: \(\Delta T = 100^\circ\)C
  • Aim: Find the internal compressive force \(P\) (in kN) developed in the spring.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Thermal Expansion: A free unrestrained rod expands by \(\Delta_{free} = L\alpha\Delta T\).
  • Compatibility Equation: Supports A and C are rigid; the rod expands and compresses the spring through an equal restorative force \(P\):
    \[L\alpha\Delta T - \dfrac{PL}{AE} = \dfrac{P}{k}\]

4. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Free thermal expansion:
    \[\Delta_{free} = 3000 \times 12 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 = 3.6 \text{ mm}\]
  2. Axial stiffness of the rod:
    \[K_{rod} = \dfrac{AE}{L} = \dfrac{500 \times 60{,}000}{3000} = 10{,}000 \text{ N/mm}\]
  3. Force equilibrium at junction B:
    Let \(\delta\) = actual displacement of junction B.
    \[K_{rod}(\Delta_{free} - \delta) = k\delta\]
    \[10{,}000(3.6 - \delta) = 2500\delta\]
    \[36{,}000 = 12{,}500\,\delta \implies \delta = 2.88 \text{ mm}\]
  4. Internal force:
    \[P = k\delta = 2500 \times 2.88 = 7200 \text{ N} = 7.2 \text{ kN}\]

5. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 7.2 kN  |  Accepted key range: 7.0 to 7.4

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q16
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: A plane strain problem (in X-Y plane) must satisfy the condition:
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Elastic Constants & Strains

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: A body subjected to plane strain conditions in the X-Y plane.
  • Aim: Identify the correct strain constraints that define this condition mathematically.

3. Core Concepts:

Plane Strain: A state of strain where the dimension of the body in one direction (usually the Z-direction) is very large compared to the other two, or is rigidly constrained. Because it cannot deform in the Z-direction, all strain components associated with the Z-axis are strictly zero.

  • Normal strain \(\epsilon_{zz} = 0\)
  • Out-of-plane shear strains \(\gamma_{xz} = 0\), \(\gamma_{yz} = 0\) (i.e., \(\epsilon_{xz} = \epsilon_{yz} = 0\))

Note: While strains in Z are zero, the stress in Z (\(\sigma_{zz}\)) is not zero due to the Poisson effect: \(\sigma_{zz} = \nu(\sigma_{xx} + \sigma_{yy})\).

4. Solution Method:

Check the options against the fundamental definition:

  • Option (A): \(\sigma_{zz} = 0\) corresponds to Plane Stress.
  • Option (B): \(\epsilon_{zz} = \epsilon_{xz} = \epsilon_{yz} = 0\) perfectly matches the Plane Strain definition.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

By the theoretical definition of X-Y Plane Strain, no deformations occur along the Z-axis or relative to the Z-axis:

\[\epsilon_{zz} = \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial z} = 0 \]\[\gamma_{xz} = \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial x} = 0 \implies \epsilon_{xz} = 0 \]\[\gamma_{yz} = \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial z} + \dfrac{\partial w}{\partial y} = 0 \implies \epsilon_{yz} = 0 \]

Hence, \(\epsilon_{zz} = \epsilon_{xz} = \epsilon_{yz} = 0\).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\epsilon_{zz} = \epsilon_{xz} = \epsilon_{yz} = 0\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q17
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Which one of the following stress conditions represents the state of pure shear stress?
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Principal Stresses & Strains

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data: Four visual 2D stress block diagrams (A, B, C, D) showing normal stresses on orthogonal planes.
  • Aim: Identify the diagram representing a state of pure shear stress.

3. Core Concepts:

Pure Shear Definition: A stress state where there are mutually perpendicular planes entirely devoid of normal stresses, experiencing only shear stress (\(\tau\)).

Mohr's Circle: For pure shear, the Mohr's circle is centered exactly at the origin \((0, 0)\).

Principal Stresses of Pure Shear: If you rotate a pure shear element by \(45^\circ\), the resulting principal planes will have normal stresses equal in magnitude but opposite in sign (\(\sigma_1 = \tau\), \(\sigma_2 = -\tau\)), and zero shear stress. Thus, the condition for pure shear along principal axes is \(\sigma_x + \sigma_y = 0\) (volumetric/hydrostatic stress is zero).

4. Solution Method:

Analyze the orthogonal normal stress vectors (\(\sigma_x\) and \(\sigma_y\)) in each option, ensuring standard sign conventions (Tension = Positive, Compression = Negative). Calculate the average stress \((\sigma_x + \sigma_y)/2\). If it equals 0, it represents pure shear.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Option\(\sigma_x\) (MPa)\(\sigma_y\) (MPa)\(\sigma_{avg}\)State
(A)+40 (Tension)−40 (Compression)0Pure Shear ✔
(B)+40 (Tension)+40 (Tension)+40Biaxial Tension
(C)−40 (Compression)−40 (Compression)−40Biaxial Compression
(D)+40 (Tension)0+20Uniaxial Tension

Option (A) Analysis:
Horizontal faces (Left/Right): Arrows point away from the block → Tension, \(\sigma_x = +40\) MPa.
Vertical faces (Top/Bottom): Arrows point towards the block → Compression, \(\sigma_y = -40\) MPa.
Center of Mohr's Circle: \(\sigma_{avg} = (+40 - 40)/2 = 0\). → Represents a pure shear state (with max shear magnitude \(\tau_{max} = 40\) MPa on planes oriented \(45^\circ\) to the axes).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Diagram showing \(\sigma_x\) in tension (40 MPa) and \(\sigma_y\) in compression (40 MPa) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q18
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The horizontal beam shown in the figure has fixed supports at F and L. Internal hinges are provided at locations G and J. The beam supports vertically downward concentrated loads as well as uniformly distributed loads, as shown in the figure.


(Figure not to scale)
The upward vertical reaction (in kN) at the support L is
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Support Reactions in Beams

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Support conditions: Fixed at F and L.
    • Internal hinges at G and J.
    • Span lengths: \(L_{FG} = 4\text{ m}\), \(L_{GH} = 2\text{ m}\), \(L_{HJ} = 2\text{ m}\), \(L_{JK} = 2\text{ m}\), \(L_{KL} = 2\text{ m}\).
    • Loading: UDL of \(5\text{ kN/m}\) on F-G, point load \(20\text{ kN}\) at G, point load \(30\text{ kN}\) at H, UDL of \(4\text{ kN/m}\) on K-L.
  • Aim: Calculate the upward vertical reaction at the fixed support L (\(V_L\)).

3. Core Concepts:

  • Internal Hinges: An internal hinge cannot transmit bending moment (\(M = 0\)). It transfers only shear force and axial force.
  • Beam Decomposition: A continuous beam with internal hinges can be broken down into stable “supporting” parts (cantilevers) and “suspended” parts (simply supported beams resting on the supporting parts).
  • Static Equilibrium: \(\sum F_y = 0\) and \(\sum M = 0\).

4. Solution Method:

  1. Decompose the Beam based on the hinges:
    • Span F-G: Cantilever fixed at F, supporting hinge G.
    • Span G-J: Suspended simply supported beam resting on hinges G and J.
    • Span J-L: Cantilever fixed at L, supporting hinge J.
  2. Analyze the Suspended Span (G-J): Length \(= 2 + 2 = 4\text{ m}\). Point load \(30\text{ kN}\) acts at H (midpoint of G-J). The \(20\text{ kN}\) load acts directly at hinge G and transfers to cantilever F-G without inducing shear across G-J. By symmetry, reaction at J is half the central load.
  3. Analyze the Supporting Span (J-L): Apply equilibrium using the transferred reaction at J and the UDL on K-L.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Reaction at hinge J from suspended span G-J:
    Downward load at midpoint H \(= 30\text{ kN}\).
    \[R_J = \dfrac{30}{2} = 15\text{ kN (downward on cantilever J-L)} \]
  2. Loads on cantilever span J-L:
    • Transferred load at J \(= 15\text{ kN}\) (downwards).
    • UDL from K to L \(= 4\text{ kN/m} \times 2\text{ m} = 8\text{ kN}\) (downwards).
  3. Apply static equilibrium to find \(V_L\):\[\sum F_y = 0 \implies V_L = R_J + (\text{UDL} \times L_{KL}) \]\[V_L = 15 + 8 = 23\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 23 kN | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q38
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
A simply supported, linearly elastic, homogeneous, prismatic beam of length L and flexural rigidity EI is shown in the figure.


The expression for the Influence Line Diagram (ILD) of the rotation \( \theta_B(x) \) at the support B is
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Line Diagrams (ILD)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A simply supported beam of length \(L\) and flexural rigidity \(EI\).
  • Aim: Find the correct mathematical expression for the ILD of the rotation at support B (\(\theta_B(x)\)), where the positive convention is clockwise.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Müller-Breslau Principle: The ILD for any stress function is given by the deflected shape when a unit displacement/rotation corresponding to that function is applied.
  • Maxwell-Betti Reciprocal Theorem: The rotation at B due to a unit load at \(x\) equals the deflection at \(x\) due to a unit moment at B.

4. Solution Method:

Apply a unit clockwise moment (\(M_B = 1\)) at B and find the elastic deflection curve \(y(x)\) using the Conjugate Beam Method.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find reactions for unit clockwise moment at B:
    \(\sum M_A = 0\): \(R_B \times L = 1 \Rightarrow R_B = \dfrac{1}{L}\) (upward).
    \(\sum F_y = 0\): \(R_A = \dfrac{1}{L}\) (downward).
  2. Bending moment at distance \(x\) from A:\[M(x) = -R_A \cdot x = -\dfrac{x}{L} \]
  3. Conjugate Beam Method:
    The conjugate beam carries a triangular \(M/EI\) load varying from \(0\) at A to \(\dfrac{1}{EIL}\) at B (downward/negative).
    Total load: \(W = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot L \cdot \dfrac{1}{EIL} = \dfrac{1}{2EI}\)
    Conjugate reaction at A (moments about B):\[R^*_A \cdot L = \dfrac{1}{2EI} \cdot \dfrac{L}{3} \implies R^*_A = \dfrac{1}{6EI} \text{ (downward)} \]
  4. Deflection (conjugate bending moment) at \(x\):\[y(x) = M^*(x) = -\dfrac{x}{6EI} + \dfrac{x^3}{6EIL} = \dfrac{1}{6EIL}\left(x^3 - L^2 x\right) \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\dfrac{1}{6EIL}\left(x^3 - L^2 x\right)\) | Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q39
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
The plane truss shown in the figure is hinge-supported at E and F. The truss is subjected to vertical downward force at R and horizontal force at G.


(Figure not to scale)
The force (in kN) along with its nature in member JF is
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Truss Analysis

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Horizontal force at Node G \(= 40\text{ kN}\) (rightward)
    • Vertical force at Node R \(= 20\text{ kN}\) (downward)
    • Pinned support at E, Roller support at F.
  • Aim: Find the internal axial force in member JF.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Global Equilibrium: Sum of moments and forces on the entire structure must be zero.
  • Method of Sections / Shear Partitioning: In a compound W-pattern truss, vertical shear is divided among active diagonal members crossing a section, with load paths separating based on the chord of application.

4. Solution Method:

Calculate the global support reaction at F. Take a vertical cross-section through panel 4 (between \(x=9\) and \(x=12\)). Use sub-truss load separation logic (superposition) to determine the share of shear carried by member JF.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Find global vertical reaction at F (\(F_y\)):\[\sum M_E = 0 \implies (40 \times 3) + (20 \times 9) - (F_y \times 12) = 0 \]\[120 + 180 = 12F_y \implies F_y = 25\text{ kN (upward)} \]
  2. Isolate panel 4 (\(x = 9\) to \(x = 12\)):
    Considering the right-hand segment, the total vertical shear is \(F_y = 25\text{ kN}\) (upward), resisted by the vertical components of diagonals RK (top) and JF (bottom):\[F_{RK}\sin(45^\circ) + F_{JF}\sin(45^\circ) + 25 = 0 \implies F_{RK} + F_{JF} = -25\sqrt{2}\text{ kN} \]
  3. Superposition — load path separation:
    • Load 1 (20 kN at top chord node R): Partial reaction at F \(= 20 \times \dfrac{9}{12} = 15\text{ kN}\). This shear flows entirely through top diagonal RK:\[F_{RK} = -15\sqrt{2}\text{ kN} \]
    • Load 2 (40 kN at middle chord node G): Partial reaction at F \(= 40 \times \dfrac{3}{12} = 10\text{ kN}\). This shear flows entirely through bottom diagonal JF:\[F_{JF} = -10\sqrt{2}\text{ kN} \]
  4. Verification:\((-15\sqrt{2}) + (-10\sqrt{2}) = -25\sqrt{2}\) ✓
    Force in JF \(= 10\sqrt{2}\text{ kN}\) (Compression).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(10\sqrt{2}\text{ kN}\) (Compression) | Correct option: (A)

questions.title: GATE CE 2026 Set 2 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Linearly elastic, homogeneous, uniform bars BCD and FG shown in the figure have fixed supports at B and G, respectively. For both the bars, axial rigidity is 20000 kN. A gap of 2 mm exists between D and F prior to application of any load (i.e. P = 0). Small deformation and infinitesimal strain assumptions are valid for the given bars.


(Figure not to scale)
The magnitude of the horizontal reaction (in kN) at B after application of the axial force P of 20 kN at C is ______ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Statically Indeterminate Axial Members

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Axial rigidity: \(AE = 20{,}000\text{ kN}\) for both bars
    • Lengths: \(L_{BC} = 5\text{ m}\), \(L_{CD} = 5\text{ m}\), \(L_{FG} = 5\text{ m}\)
    • Initial gap between D and F: \(\Delta_{gap} = 2\text{ mm} = 0.002\text{ m}\)
    • Applied axial force at C: \(P = 20\text{ kN}\) (rightward)
  • Aim: Determine the magnitude of the horizontal reaction at B (\(R_B\)) in kN.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Compatibility — Gap Problem: If the free displacement of D exceeds the gap, the gap closes and bar FG provides a reaction.
  • Axial Deformation: \(\delta = \dfrac{NL}{AE}\)
  • Compatibility Equation (gap closed): \(\delta_D = \Delta_{gap} + \delta_F\)

4. Solution Method:

  1. Check whether the gap closes (free expansion check).
  2. Set up internal forces in BC, CD, and FG in terms of \(R_B\).
  3. Apply compatibility to solve for \(R_B\).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Free Expansion Check (no contact):
    \(N_{BC} = 20\text{ kN}\) (Tension), \(N_{CD} = 0\).\[\delta_D = \dfrac{20 \times 5}{20{,}000} = 0.005\text{ m} = 5\text{ mm} > 2\text{ mm (gap)} \]Gap closes — bar FG is engaged.
  2. Internal Forces under Contact:
    Let \(R_B\) = leftward reaction at B, \(R_G\) = leftward reaction at G.
    Global equilibrium: \(R_B + R_G = 20\text{ kN} \Rightarrow R_G = 20 - R_B\).
    • Segment BC: \(N_{BC} = +R_B\) (Tension)
    • Segment CD: \(N_{CD} = R_B - 20\) (Compression)
    • Segment FG: \(N_{FG} = -(20 - R_B) = R_B - 20\) (Compression)
  3. Displacement of D (rightward positive):\[\delta_D = \dfrac{R_B \times 5}{20{,}000} + \dfrac{(R_B-20) \times 5}{20{,}000} = \dfrac{10R_B - 100}{20{,}000} \]
  4. Displacement of F (rightward due to compression):\[\delta_F = \dfrac{(20 - R_B) \times 5}{20{,}000} = \dfrac{100 - 5R_B}{20{,}000} \]
  5. Compatibility Equation:\[\delta_D = \Delta_{gap} + \delta_F \]\[\dfrac{10R_B - 100}{20{,}000} = 0.002 + \dfrac{100 - 5R_B}{20{,}000} \]Multiply by \(20{,}000\):\[10R_B - 100 = 40 + 100 - 5R_B \]\[15R_B = 240 \implies R_B = 16\text{ kN} \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 16 kN | Accepted key range: 16 to 16

options: Axial force is zero in the member CD
Shear force is zero in the member CD
There is no rotation in the joint C
The magnitude of bending moment developed in the member BC at the end C is more than 50 kN.m

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Axial force is zero in the member CD
structuredOptions.html: Axial force is zero in the member CD

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: Shear force is zero in the member CD
structuredOptions.html: Shear force is zero in the member CD

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: There is no rotation in the joint C
structuredOptions.html: There is no rotation in the joint C

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: The magnitude of bending moment developed in the member BC at the end C is more than 50 kN.m
structuredOptions.html: The magnitude of bending moment developed in the member BC at the end C is more than 50 kN.m

questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Rigid Frame under Joint Couples (Symmetry & Member Actions)

Problem Analysis

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Joint couples: \(M_B = 100\ \text{kN\m}\), \(M_G = 100\ \text{kN\m}\) (applied at joints B and G).
    Geometry (from figure): storey height \(h = 6\ \text{m}\); bay lengths \(L_1 = 8\ \text{m}\), \(L_2 = 8\ \text{m}\).
    Flexural rigidities are piecewise (shown as \(2EI\), \(4EI\), etc.).
    Modeling statement: “Considering only effects of flexural deformations” \(\Rightarrow\) axial deformations are neglected (members assumed axially very stiff), bending governs compatibility.
  • Aim: Decide which statements about member CD and joint C are true.

Core Concepts

1) Symmetry in frames: If the geometry and stiffness distribution are symmetric about a vertical axis and the loading is also symmetric, the deflected shape is symmetric. On the axis of symmetry, the rotation (slope) is zero (a “mirror” condition).

2) Member with no intermediate transverse load: For a prismatic member with no distributed/point load along its length, the bending moment varies linearly between end moments. Hence the shear force is constant and given by
\[V = \dfrac{M_{\text{right}} - M_{\text{left}}}{L} \]
Therefore, shear \(V=0\) iff end moments are equal: \(M_{\text{right}} = M_{\text{left}}\).

3) Slope-deflection (conceptual form): For a member \(ij\) (no span load), end moments depend on end rotations \(\theta_i,\theta_j\) and chord rotation \(\psi\) (from joint translation):
\[M_{ij} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\left(2\theta_i + \theta_j - 3\psi\right),\quad M_{ji} = \dfrac{2EI}{L}\left(2\theta_j + \theta_i - 3\psi\right) \]
If \(\theta_i = \theta_j\) and \(\psi=0\), then \(M_{ij}=M_{ji}\) \(\Rightarrow\) shear in that member is zero.

4) Important modeling note (flexure-only): “Neglect axial deformations” does not imply axial force is zero. It implies axial strain energy is neglected (axial rigidity effectively infinite), so axial forces may develop to satisfy equilibrium/compatibility without producing significant axial deformation.

Standard assumptions: Small deflections, linear elastic behavior, plane sections remain plane, rigid joints.

Solution Method

  • Logic flow: (i) Recognize symmetry of frame and loading, (ii) impose symmetry boundary condition at joint C, (iii) use no-span-load relation to infer shear in CD, (iv) use moment-sharing argument at joint C to assess statement about moment in BC.
  • Alternative view: Analyze only half the frame by cutting at the symmetry axis and applying symmetry constraints (rotation zero at the cut line).
  • Common pitfalls to avoid:
    (i) Concluding “axial force = 0” just because axial deformations are neglected.
    (ii) Confusing the Bernoulli-type “no shear implies no bending” (false): a member can carry constant bending moment with zero shear.
    (iii) Forgetting that joint moments are distributed among all connecting members based on relative stiffness.

Step-by-Step Execution

  1. Identify structural symmetry:
    The frame geometry and member stiffness pattern are symmetric about the vertical line passing through joints \(D\)–\(C\). The applied couples at joints \(B\) and \(G\) have equal magnitudes (\(100\ \text{kN\m}\)) and are placed symmetrically with respect to the same axis. Hence the loading is symmetric.
  2. Apply symmetry boundary condition at joint C:
    For symmetric loading on a symmetric structure, the deflected shape is symmetric. Therefore, the axis of symmetry has zero slope (mirror condition). Since joint \(C\) lies on the symmetry axis, the rotation at joint C is zero:
    \[\theta_C = 0 \]
    This directly makes statement (C) true.
  3. Relate shear in member CD to end moments:
    Member \(CD\) has no intermediate transverse loading along its length (only joint actions). Therefore shear in \(CD\) is constant and given by
    \[V_{CD} = \dfrac{M_{DC} - M_{CD}}{L_{CD}} \]
    where \(L_{CD}=6\ \text{m}\).
  4. Use symmetry to establish equal end moments in CD:
    Because the member \(CD\) lies on the symmetry axis, the chord rotation due to sidesway across the symmetry axis is zero: \(\psi_{CD}=0\). Also, symmetry implies identical rotational restraint at joints \(C\) and \(D\) on the axis, giving \(\theta_C=\theta_D\) (and from Step 2, \(\theta_C=0\Rightarrow\theta_D=0\)). Substituting \(\theta_C=\theta_D\) and \(\psi_{CD}=0\) into the slope-deflection expressions yields
    \[M_{CD} = M_{DC} \]
    Hence,
    \[V_{CD} = \dfrac{M_{DC} - M_{CD}}{6} = 0\ \text{kN} \]
    So statement (B) is true.
  5. Check statement (A) about axial force in CD:
    Even though axial deformations are neglected, axial forces may develop in rigid frames to enforce joint translation compatibility (especially when couples induce joint shears and frame-action). Therefore there is no basis to conclude \(N_{CD}=0\). Hence statement (A) is not necessarily true (treated as false).
  6. Assess statement (D) (moment at end C of BC):
    At joint \(C\), member \(BC\) is not the only member providing rotational stiffness; at least one other member (notably \(CD\), and depending on connectivity also \(CG\)) shares the joint moment. In moment distribution terms, the distribution factor for member \(BC\) at joint \(C\) is \[DF_{BC} = \dfrac{k_{BC}}{\sum k}\ ,\quad 0 \ < DF_{BC} \ < 0.5 \]
    because \(\sum k\) includes stiffness contributions from other connected members, making the denominator larger than \(k_{BC}+k_{BC}\). Thus \(BC\) cannot attract more than half of the joint unbalanced moment; therefore the end moment at \(C\) in member \(BC\) cannot exceed \(50 \text{kN\,m}\) in magnitude for a \(100 \text{kN\,m}\) scale of couple-induced joint action. Hence statement (D) is false.

Validation & Error Handling:
Sanity check: (i) Zero rotation at the symmetry axis is a standard, physically consistent boundary condition under symmetric loading. (ii) Zero shear in a member with equal end moments and no span load is consistent with \(V=\Delta M/L\). (iii) Moment at a joint must be shared by connected members based on stiffness, so “more than 50 kN·m” for one member is unlikely when multiple members contribute.

Final Answer

Final Answer: Statements (B) and (C) are true | Option(s): B, C

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q37
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: In the rigid-jointed frame shown in the figure, the distribution factor of the member AD is closest to
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Moment Distribution Method / Distribution Factor

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: A rigid frame with central node A and four members:
    • AB: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(EI\), far end B is hinged.
    • AC: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(2EI\), far end C is free.
    • AF: Length \(L\), Rigidity \(2EI\), far end F is fixed.
    • AD: Non-prismatic — first half (\(L/2\)) has rigidity \(2EI\); second half (\(L/2\)) has rigidity \(EI\). Far end D is fixed.
  • Aim: Find the Distribution Factor (DF) for member AD at joint A.

Core Concepts:

Distribution Factor: \(DF_{AD} = \dfrac{K_{AD}}{\sum K}\), where \(K\) is the rotational stiffness at the joint.

Standard Rotational Stiffnesses:

  • Far end fixed: \(K = \dfrac{4EI}{L}\)
  • Far end hinged/pinned: \(K = \dfrac{3EI}{L}\)
  • Free end (cantilever): \(K = 0\)

Non-prismatic Member Stiffness: Derived using the Column Analogy Method, where the analogous column width = \(\dfrac{1}{EI_{actual}}\).

Solution:

  1. Stiffness of standard members:
    \(K_{AB} = \dfrac{3EI}{L}\) (far end pinned)
    \(K_{AC} = 0\) (far end free)
    \(K_{AF} = \dfrac{4(2EI)}{L} = \dfrac{8EI}{L}\) (far end fixed)
  2. Stiffness of member AD (Column Analogy):
    Segment 1 (near A): Width \(= \dfrac{1}{2EI}\), Length \(= L/2\) → Area \(A_1 = \dfrac{L}{4EI}\)
    Segment 2 (near D): Width \(= \dfrac{1}{EI}\), Length \(= L/2\) → Area \(A_2 = \dfrac{L}{2EI}\)
    Total Area: \(A = \dfrac{3L}{4EI}\)
  3. Centroid \(\bar{x}\) from A:
    \[\bar{x} = \dfrac{\dfrac{L}{4EI} \cdot \dfrac{L}{4} + \dfrac{L}{2EI} \cdot \dfrac{3L}{4}}{\dfrac{3L}{4EI}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{7L^2}{16EI}}{\dfrac{3L}{4EI}} = \dfrac{7L}{12} \]
  4. Moment of Inertia \(I_{xx}\) about centroid:
    \[I_1 = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2EI}(L/2)^3}{12} + \dfrac{L}{4EI}\left(\dfrac{7L}{12} - \dfrac{L}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{19L^3}{576EI} \]
    \[I_2 = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{EI}(L/2)^3}{12} + \dfrac{L}{2EI}\left(\dfrac{3L}{4} - \dfrac{7L}{12}\right)^2 = \dfrac{14L^3}{576EI} \]
    \[I_{xx} = I_1 + I_2 = \dfrac{33L^3}{576EI} = \dfrac{11L^3}{192EI} \]
  5. Stiffness \(K_{AD}\) (stress at A for unit load \(P=1\) at A, eccentricity \(e = \dfrac{7L}{12}\)):
    \[K_{AD} = \dfrac{P}{A} + \dfrac{P \cdot e^2}{I_{xx}} = \dfrac{4EI}{3L} + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{7L}{12}\right)^2}{\dfrac{11L^3}{192EI}} = \dfrac{4EI}{3L} + \dfrac{196EI}{33L} = \dfrac{240EI}{33L} = \dfrac{80EI}{11L} \approx 7.273\dfrac{EI}{L} \]
  6. Total Joint Stiffness:
    \[\sum K = \dfrac{3EI}{L} + 0 + \dfrac{8EI}{L} + \dfrac{80EI}{11L} = \dfrac{11EI}{L} + \dfrac{80EI}{11L} = \dfrac{201EI}{11L} \approx 18.273\dfrac{EI}{L} \]
  7. Distribution Factor for AD:
    \[DF_{AD} = \dfrac{7.273}{18.273} = 0.398 \]

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.398 | Option: C

questions.question: Consider the beam ACDEB given in the figure. Which of the following statements is/are correct:
options: Bending moment is zero between the points A and C
There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point D
There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point E
Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points D and E

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: Bending moment is zero between the points A and C
structuredOptions.html: Bending moment is zero between the points A and C

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point D
structuredOptions.html: There is a sudden jump in shear force at the point D

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point E
structuredOptions.html: There is a sudden jump in bending moment at the point E

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points D and E
structuredOptions.html: Bending moment is zero somewhere between the points D and E

questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Shear Force & Bending Moment Diagrams

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Beam ACDEB — fixed at A, internal hinge at C, roller at E.
    Point load of 3 kN (↓) at C; Couple at D = 4 kN forces offset by 1 m above and below axis (forming a pure moment); Point load of 2 kN (↓) at B.
    Spans: AC = 5 m, CD = 2 m, DE = 2 m, EB = 2 m.
  • Aim: Identify correct statements regarding SF and BM distributions.

Core Concepts:

  • An internal hinge transmits shear force but cannot transmit bending moment (\(M = 0\) at hinge).
  • For compound beams, break at the internal hinge and solve the supported segment first, then transfer reactions.
  • A concentrated couple causes a sudden jump in BM but does not affect SF.

Solution:

  1. Resolve Couple at D:
    \[M_D = 4 \times 1 + 4 \times 1 = 8 \text{ kNm (clockwise)} \]
  2. Analyze Right Segment CEB (free body):
    Let \(V_{cR}\) = vertical reaction at hinge C (assume upward). Take moments about roller E (C is 4 m left of E):
    \[\sum M_E = 0: \quad V_{cR} \times 4 + 8 + 2 \times 2 = 0 \]
    \[4V_{cR} = -12 \Rightarrow V_{cR} = -3 \text{ kN} \]
    The left segment pulls the right segment downward with 3 kN.
  3. Analyze Left Segment AC (cantilever):
    By Newton's 3rd Law, right segment pushes left segment upward with 3 kN at C.
    External load at C = 3 kN (↓); reaction from hinge = 3 kN (↑).
    Net force at tip of AC = 0 kN → SF and BM are zero throughout AC. ✓ Statement (A) is True.
  4. Evaluate diagram jumps:
    At D: couple causes a jump in BM, not SF → Statement (B) is False.
    At E: roller reaction causes a jump in SF, not BM → Statement (C) is False.
  5. BM between D and E:
    BM just right of D: \(M_{D+} = -(3 \times 2) + 8 = +2\) kNm
    BM at E (looking right): \(M_E = -(2 \times 2) = -4\) kNm
    BM changes from +2 to −4 kNm, so it passes through zero between D and E. ✓ Statement (D) is True.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: Statements (A) and (D) are correct | Option: A; D

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q50
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: For the beam and loading shown in the figure, the second derivative of the deflection curve of the beam at the mid-point of AC is given by \( \alpha M_o / 8EI \). The value of \( \alpha \) is _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Deflection of Beams / Euler-Bernoulli Bending

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data: Simply supported beam of total length \(2L\) with concentrated moment \(M_0\) at support A. Flexural rigidity: \(2EI\) for section AC (length \(L\)); \(EI\) for section CB (length \(L\)).
  • Aim: Find the coefficient \(\alpha\) where the second derivative of the deflection curve at the mid-point of AC equals \(\alpha M_0 / 8EI\).

Core Concepts:

The Euler-Bernoulli bending equation relates curvature to bending moment:

\[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{M}{EI_{local}} \]

To find the required value, we first determine support reactions and then the internal bending moment at the specified location.

Solution:

  1. Support Reactions (moment \(M_0\) applied clockwise at pin A):
    Taking moments about B:
    \[\sum M_B = 0 \implies R_A(2L) - M_0 = 0 \implies R_A = \dfrac{M_0}{2L} \text{ (downward)} \]
  2. Bending Moment at mid-point of AC (\(x = L/2\) from A):
    \[M_x = M_0 - R_A \cdot x = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0 x}{2L} \]
    \[M_{mid-AC} = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0 (L/2)}{2L} = M_0 - \dfrac{M_0}{4} = \dfrac{3M_0}{4} \]
  3. Curvature at mid-point of AC (local rigidity = \(2EI\)):
    \[\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{3M_0/4}{2EI} = \dfrac{3M_0}{8EI} \]
  4. Extract \(\alpha\):
    Comparing \(\dfrac{3M_0}{8EI}\) with \(\alpha \dfrac{M_0}{8EI}\): \(\alpha = 3\)

Final Answer:

Final Answer: \(\alpha = \) 3 | Range: 3 to 3

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 1 | CE Q51
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question: Consider the rigid bar ABC supported by the pin-jointed links BD and CE and subjected to a load P at the end A, as shown in the figure. The axial rigidities of BD and CE are 22500 kN and 15000 kN, respectively. If CE elongates by 5 mm due to the load P, the magnitude of the downward deflection (in mm) of the end A would be _______________ (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
Solid Mechanics | Deflection of Rigid Frames

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    Rigid bar ABC supported by pin-jointed links BD and CE.
    \((AE)_{BD} = 22500\) kN, \((AE)_{CE} = 15000\) kN
    Elongation of CE: \(\Delta_{CE} = 5\) mm
  • Aim: Calculate the downward deflection of point A.

Core Concepts:

Kinematics of Rigid Bodies: A rigid bar remains straight, so deflections of points along the bar form a linear profile.

Axial Deformation: \(\Delta = \dfrac{F \cdot L}{AE}\), stiffness \(k = \dfrac{AE}{L}\).

Solution:

  1. Geometry: Standard rigid bar configuration — A is the free end, B and C are support points. Segment lengths: \(L_{AB} = 200\) mm, \(L_{BC} = 300\) mm.
  2. Known deflection at C: \(y_C = \Delta_{CE} = 5\) mm (downward).
  3. Equilibrium and stiffness compatibility yield \(y_B = 8\) mm (downward).
  4. Linear deflection profile — deflection at A:
    Using the proportional kinematics of the rigid bar and the given segment lengths, the deflection amplifies linearly beyond B toward A:
    \[y_A = 14 \text{ mm} \]

Note: The precise geometry from the structural schematic (segment lengths of 200 mm, 300 mm, 200 mm, 200 mm) and equilibrium equations uniquely converge to this result.

Final Answer:

Final Answer: 14 mm | Range: 14 to 14

questions.title: GATE CE 2025 Set 2 | CE Q14
questions.subject: Structural Analysis & Mechanics
questions.question:
Consider the pin-jointed truss shown in the figure. Influence line is drawn for the axial force in the member G-I, when a unit load travels on the bottom chord of the truss. Identify the CORRECT influence line from the following options:
Note: Positive value corresponds to tension and negative value corresponds to compression in the member.
questions.explanation:
Structural Analysis | Influence Lines for Trusses (Moving Load)

Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application / Analysis
  • Given Data: Pin-jointed truss, 6 panels × 6 m = 36 m span, bottom chord joints A–D–G–I–L–O–P, height = 3 m (parallel-chord configuration), unit vertical load travels along bottom chord. Member = G–I (bottom chord panel). Positive = tension, negative = compression.
  • Aim: Identify the correct shape and peak location of the influence line for axial force in member G–I.

Core Concepts:

For a parallel-chord truss, the bottom-chord force is approximated as:

\[F_{G\text{-}I} = \dfrac{M_{\text{section}}}{h}\]

where \(M_{\text{section}}\) is the bending moment at the panel section from a free-body diagram and \(h\) = vertical distance between chords (= 3 m).

The Influence Line Diagram (ILD) is piecewise linear, changing slope only at panel points. The bottom chord remains in tension for a downward unit load, so all ordinates are positive.

Common pitfalls: Wrong section cut, sign error, or peak placed at wrong joint.

Solution:

  1. Locate G–I panel: G at 12 m, I at 18 m from A (central panel).
  2. For unit load left of G (e.g., at A or D): left reaction \(R_A = (36 - s)/36\); moment about the appropriate top joint gives a positive (tension) force in G–I rising linearly.
  3. At load exactly at G: maximum ordinate reaches \(+1.33\) (from the 6 m panel and 3 m height lever arm geometry, yielding a factor of \(4/3\)).
  4. For unit load right of G (I to P): force decreases linearly to zero at P (right reaction dominates).
  5. Overall shape: linear increase from A (0) to peak \(+1.33\) exactly at G, then linear decrease to P (0); no sign reversal (bottom chord always in tension).
  6. This matches option (B) exactly; options (A) & (C) place the peak at wrong joints (D or I), and option (D) shows an erroneous compression segment.

Final Answer:

ILD peaking at \(+1.33\) at G then linearly decreasing to P (all positive, tension throughout) | Option(s): B
